justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 310.5 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 315 at the one-month horizon. This gentle positive slope was driven by a baseline assumption of mean-reverting behavior around a slightly elevated trend, consistent with modest macroeconomic tailwinds and no immediate catalysts for a sharp reversal. The one-day estimate anchors closely to the last observed value, with the small premium over that level reflecting typical overnight drift and momentum. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, I incorporated a modest continuation of prevailing conditions, though I deliberately kept the upward slope shallow to avoid over-extrapolating short-term trends into longer periods where reversion forces tend to dominate.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the fundamental compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 19-point range is relatively tight because near-term price behavior is constrained by recent volatility clustering and the absence of scheduled high-impact events in the immediate window. By one week, the range widens to 36 points, capturing the increased likelihood of interim data releases, policy signals, or sentiment shifts that could meaningfully redirect the trajectory. At one month, the 70-point range acknowledges that a full calendar month contains numerous potential inflection points — earnings announcements, central bank meetings, geopolitical developments — any of which could drive the outcome well away from the point estimate.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these wider stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharp inflation surprise or a sudden tightening of financial conditions — could trigger a rapid repricing that breaches the lower bound of the one-month interval. A liquidity event or contagion from a stress episode in a related market could also produce gap moves that outpace normal volatility assumptions. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected policy pivot or a resolution of a major geopolitical uncertainty could produce a surge beyond the upper bound. These tail scenarios are genuinely possible but were assigned low enough probability that they fall outside the 90% coverage range I was targeting.
